Celtic Church, Reformation and Post-Reformation Church: Controversy and authority; missionary outreach; developments and outreach in Christianity

5 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Why did a king and queen keep Easter on different days, and how did a meeting settle it?
  2. Mission 2Patrick never mentions Armagh, so how did it become the head church of all Ireland?
  3. Mission 3Why would a monk leave home forever, sailing off with no plan to return?

Mission 1

Mission 1: Why did a king and queen keep Easter on different days, and how did a meeting settle it?

Make a guess: Why did a king and queen keep Easter on different days, and how did a meeting settle it?

Mission 1

Why the date of Easter mattered

  • Easter (Latin Pascha, from Hebrew Pesach, Passover) celebrates Christ's resurrection, the centre of Christian faith.
  • Jesus died at Passover, kept on the 14th day of the first month (Exodus 12:6), a lunar date. "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place." (1 Corinthians 5:7, WEBBE)
  • So the date depends on the moon and the spring equinox, and must fall on a Sunday (the day of resurrection).
  • Lent (fasting) leads up to it; the whole church year hangs on it.
  • Keeping Easter together was a sign of unity: different dates meant one group feasting while another still fasted.
Mission 1

The wider controversy

  • Second century: some churches in Asia Minor kept Easter on the 14th day of the moon, whatever the weekday (Quartodecimans, "fourteenth-ers"); Rome kept the following Sunday.
  • Polycarp and Pope Anicetus (c. 155) agreed to differ; Pope Victor (c. 190) threatened to cut off the Asian churches; Irenaeus urged peace.
  • Council of Nicaea (325): all churches to keep Easter on the same Sunday, independently of the Jewish calendar; it left the calculation to experts.
  • Tables (cycles to predict future Easters) still differed: an 84-year cycle used in Rome and the West; the 19-year Alexandrian cycle; Victorius of Aquitaine (457); Dionysius Exiguus (525), whose Alexandrian-style tables Rome came to use.
  • The West changed its tables; churches far from Rome did not always follow.
Mission 1

The Irish practice

  • Irish and British churches kept an older 84-year table (the latercus), received in the fifth century.
  • Its rules: Easter Sunday could fall from the 14th to the 20th day of the moon; Rome's newer rules required the 15th to the 21st, with a different date for the equinox.
  • So in some years the dates differed by a week (occasionally more).
  • Opponents called the Irish Quartodecimans; Bede says this was wrong: they always kept Easter on a Sunday (HE III.4, paraphrase).
  • Tonsure: Irish monks shaved the front of the head from ear to ear; Roman monks shaved a crown (circle) on top, linked with Peter.
  • The Irish held they were faithful to the practice of their founders.
Mission 1

Ireland divides, then conforms

  • Southern Irish churches adopted the Roman reckoning c. 630, after a synod at Mag Léne and a delegation to Rome.
  • Cummian's letter (c. 632–633) to Ségéne, abbot of Iona, defends the change: unity with the universal church outweighs local custom (paraphrase).
  • Northern Irish churches and Iona (with its daughter houses in Britain) held to the old reckoning.
  • A letter from Rome (c. 640) to the northern Irish warned them over Easter (Bede, HE II.19).
  • The northern Irish churches conformed later in the seventh century; Iona only in 716.
  • So this was a debate among the Irish, not only between Ireland and Rome.
Quick check
?Why did the Irish and Roman dates for Easter sometimes differ in the seventh century?
Mission 1

Northumbria: the road to Whitby

  • King Oswald (634–642), raised in exile among the Irish, invited Aidan from Iona (635): he founded Lindisfarne. The Irish mission converted much of Northumbria.
  • King Oswiu (642–670), also raised in exile among the Irish and baptised there, kept the Irish Easter.
  • Queen Eanflæd, raised in Kent, kept the Roman Easter with her chaplain Romanus: one year the king feasted while the queen still fasted on Palm Sunday (Bede, HE III.25, paraphrase).
  • Prince Alhfrith, Oswiu's son, backed Wilfrid, a Northumbrian trained in Rome and Gaul; Wilfrid took over Ripon, sending away its Irish-trained monks.
  • Bishop Colmán of Lindisfarne (from 661) kept the Irish tradition.
  • In 664 Oswiu called a synod at Streanæshalch (Whitby), the double monastery of Abbess Hild.
Mission 1Read the source

Peter's keys

Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People (731), III.25 (paraphrase): Colmán appealed to the custom of John the Evangelist and of Columba (Colum Cille). Wilfrid replied that Rome, Italy, Gaul, Africa, Asia, Egypt and Greece kept one Easter; only the Picts and Britons, in a remote corner of the world, disagreed. Above all, the keys were given to Peter. Oswiu asked Colmán whether Christ had said this to Peter; Colmán agreed, and agreed that Columba had received no such power. Oswiu ruled for Peter, so that the keeper of heaven's gate would not turn him away.

> "I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven," (Matthew 16:18–19, WEBBE)

Q1 Which two authorities did each side appeal to?

Show answer

Colmán: John and Columba; Wilfrid: universal practice and Peter.

Q2 Why did the keys persuade Oswiu?

Show answer

Peter, holding the keys, outranked Columba; the king wanted heaven's gatekeeper on his side.

Mission 1

The main issues

  • The date of Easter: which tables and rules.
  • The tonsure: discussed in Bede (HE V.21) and Stephen of Ripon, though less fully than Easter.
  • Authority: local founders (John, Columba) or the universal church and the see of Peter.
  • Unity: one kingdom, two calendars; a church linked to Iona or to Canterbury, Gaul and Rome.
  • Behind them: politics (Oswiu's power, ties with Kent, Alhfrith's ambitions) and personalities (Wilfrid's forceful zeal).
  • Two accounts: Bede (731) and Stephen of Ripon, Life of Wilfrid (c. 715, ch. 10), which makes Wilfrid the hero.
Mission 1

Outcome

  • Oswiu decided for the Roman Easter and tonsure.
  • Colmán resigned and left with Irish monks and some English followers to Iona, then Inishbofin (an island off the west coast, now Co. Galway, 668); he founded Mayo (Co. Mayo) for the English ("Mayo of the Saxons").
  • Tuda became bishop; Eata abbot of Lindisfarne; Cuthbert accepted the Roman ways while keeping Irish holiness.
  • Wilfrid was made a bishop (consecrated in Gaul).
  • Theodore of Tarsus, archbishop of Canterbury (669), united the English church; the Synod of Hertford (672/673) fixed one Easter for all.
  • Bede still praises Aidan and the Irish monks for their holiness and poverty (HE III.5, III.26).
Quick check
?What did Colmán do after the Synod of Whitby?
Mission 1

Significance

  • For Northumbria and England: closer ties to Canterbury and the Continent; Roman church order spread; Irish influence declined but did not vanish.
  • For the Irish churches: Whitby did not decide Irish practice; Ireland changed through its own synods (south c. 630; north later; Iona 716).
  • For Bede's story: Whitby is the turning point of an English church united under Rome; he writes 67 years later, with that purpose.
  • For authority: the appeal to Peter strengthened Roman authority in the British Isles.
  • Symbolic: later writers (sometimes Protestant and nationalist) used Whitby as the "end" of an independent Celtic church.
Mission 1Diversity

Was there a "Celtic Church"?

  • Older view: a distinct Celtic Church, independent of Rome, defeated at Whitby; popular in later Protestant and romantic writing, and in some modern "Celtic spirituality".
  • Modern scholarship: Kathleen Hughes, "The Celtic Church: is this a valid concept?" (1981); Wendy Davies, "The myth of the Celtic Church" (1992):
  • Irish and British churches were in communion with Rome and respected the pope (Columbanus wrote to popes with respect, and with criticism).
  • Differences were customs (Easter tables, tonsure), not doctrine.
  • Irish churches disagreed among themselves; there was no single "Celtic" organisation.
  • The term "Celtic Church" remains in the spec as a label for the churches of Ireland and their offshoots.
Mission 1Evaluate

Whitby: Roman victory or quarrel over customs?

  • Claim: The Synod of Whitby was a decisive victory of Roman over Celtic Christianity.
  • For: Oswiu chose Rome; Colmán left; Northumbria and then all England took the Roman Easter and tonsure.
  • For: The appeal to Peter's authority carried the day, a sign of growing papal influence.
  • Against: The issue was a calendar and a haircut, not belief: both sides shared one faith.
  • Against: Much of Ireland had already conformed (c. 630); Whitby was a Northumbrian decision, and Iona changed in 716 for its own reasons.
  • Against: Politics (Oswiu's power, Kentish and Gaulish ties, Wilfrid's ambition) may matter as much as religion; Bede shapes the story.
  • Judgement criteria: Decisive for whom (Northumbria, Ireland, Iona)? About doctrine, authority or unity? How far does Bede's purpose shape the event?
Mission check

?Two churches in one town keep Christmas on different dates: one follows the Gregorian calendar (25 December), the other the Julian calendar (7 January). Both share the same creeds. Which feature of the Paschal controversy does this most closely resemble?

The Easter dispute was about calendars, custom and authority. Its heat came from the value of keeping the feast as one church.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Patrick never mentions Armagh, so how did it become the head church of all Ireland?

Make a guess: Patrick never mentions Armagh, so how did it become the head church of all Ireland?

Mission 2

What Armagh claimed

  • By the late seventh century, the church of Armagh (Irish Ard Macha, "Macha's height") claimed to be:
  • the church of Patrick, apostle of all Ireland;
  • head of all Irish churches, with a paruchia (federation) covering the whole island;
  • entitled to dues and tribute from churches founded by Patrick;
  • a court of appeal for hard cases, beneath only Rome.
  • Its leader was the coarb (comarba, heir) of Patrick: sometimes a bishop, often an abbot.
  • These are claims to primacy (first place) and jurisdiction (power to rule).
Mission 2

Patrick's own silence

  • Patrick's Confessio and Letter name no church, no Armagh, no Tara.
  • He names only the wood of Foclut by the western sea.
  • Possible link: Armagh lies near Emain Macha, the ancient royal site of the Ulaid; a bishop might well base himself near a royal centre.
  • An annal entry gives Armagh's foundation in 444, but it was probably added later.
  • Tradition also gives Saul and Downpatrick (Co. Down) as his first church and burial place: a rival focus in the north-east.
  • So Patrick's association with Armagh is possible, even likely to some historians, but not proved by first-hand evidence.
Mission 2

Background: a seventh-century contest

  • Rival federations: Kildare (Brigit), claiming to be head of almost all Irish churches (Cogitosus); Iona and its Columban houses; Clonmacnoise in the midlands.
  • Dynasties: the Uí Néill were rising as the strongest kings; Armagh lay among their Airgialla clients and allied with them. A national church suited a dynasty claiming the kingship of Tara.
  • The Easter question: Armagh joined the Roman reckoning in the later seventh century (see Mission 1); an appeal to Rome fitted that party.
  • Lost churches: Armagh's writers complained that other federations had taken churches once Patrick's.
  • Patrick's fame: the Palladius story could be told so that Patrick alone was the apostle.
Mission 2

Muirchú and Tírechán

  • Muirchú (c. 680–700): Patrick defeats the king's druids at Tara, so his authority covers all Ireland; Daire grants him the hill of Armagh after a miracle; an angel promises that Armagh will keep his honour though he dies at Saul (paraphrase).
  • Tírechán, a bishop from Connacht, Collectanea (c. 670–690): Patrick's journeys through Meath and Connacht, founding churches and ordaining bishops at each stop.
  • Purpose: to show that these churches are Patrick's, and so belong to Armagh. Tírechán complains that the communities of Columba and of Clonmacnoise have seized churches of Patrick (paraphrase).
  • Both texts read like title deeds: stories that prove ownership.
Mission 2Read the source

The Book of the Angel

The Liber Angeli (Book of the Angel), seventh century, preserved in the Book of Armagh (paraphrase):

  • An angel appears to Patrick and grants his church the whole island as its paruchia, because God gave him all the Irish.
  • Every free church and monastery in Ireland owes Armagh an honour and dues.
  • Armagh is a place of sanctuary; it holds relics of saints from Rome.
  • Appeals: any difficult case that Irish judges cannot settle is to be sent to the see of the archbishop of the Irish, Patrick, at Armagh; if it cannot be settled there, to the see of the apostle Peter in Rome.
  • Kildare: Patrick and Brigit are described as so close in love that they had one heart and one mind: a compromise that left Kildare honoured but second.

Q1 Where does the text say Armagh's authority comes from?

Show answer

A direct grant from God through an angel to Patrick.

Q2 Why might the reference to Rome strengthen Armagh's claim?

Show answer

It ties Armagh to the highest authority in the Western church, as Rome's link in Ireland.

Quick check
?Which source claims that difficult cases should be sent to Armagh, and then to Rome?
Mission 2

How the claims were promoted (1): texts and relics

  • Hagiography: Muirchú and Tírechán made Patrick the apostle of all Ireland, and Armagh his church.
  • Legal text: the Liber Angeli set out rights as if granted by God.
  • The Book of Armagh (c. 807, scribe Ferdomnach): gathered Patrick's Confessio, Muirchú, Tírechán, the Liber Angeli, a New Testament and the Life of Martin: one volume of authority.
  • Relics: the Bachall Ísu ("staff of Jesus"), said to have been Patrick's; Patrick's bell; relics of Roman saints.
  • Sanctuary: Armagh as a protected place, like the "city of refuge" Cogitosus claimed for Kildare.
Mission 2

How the claims were promoted (2): law and kings

  • The Law of Patrick (Cáin Phátraic): proclaimed over regions in the eighth and ninth centuries (e.g. 734, 737, 783 in the annals), bringing dues and protection to Armagh.
  • Circuits: the coarb of Patrick toured provinces with relics to collect tribute.
  • Uí Néill support: Armagh's rise matched the dynasty's; each strengthened the other's claim to speak for all Ireland.
  • Brian Bóruma (Boru), visiting Armagh in 1005, had a note written in the Book of Armagh confirming its rights; it calls him "imperator Scotorum" (emperor of the Irish). He was buried at Armagh in 1014.
  • Twelfth-century reform: the Synod of Kells (1152) made Armagh one of four archbishoprics and its archbishop primate.
Quick check
?Why was the 1005 note in the Book of Armagh important for Armagh's claims?
Mission 2

How valid were the claims?

  • Weak points: Patrick's own writings are silent; Palladius and others came before him; Patrick did not reach all Ireland.
  • Partisan sources: Muirchú, Tírechán and the Liber Angeli were written for Armagh, two centuries after Patrick.
  • Possible fabrication: churches "founded by Patrick" may have been other founders' (even Palladius'), absorbed into Patrick's legend (O'Rahilly, Binchy).
  • Strong points: a genuine Patrick–Armagh link is plausible (royal site, early tradition by the 600s); Patrick was the best-known early bishop; the claims were accepted by kings, churches and finally Rome.
  • Scholars: Richard Sharpe (1954–2020), "St Patrick and the see of Armagh" (1982); T. M. Charles-Edwards, Early Christian Ireland (2000): the claims grew in the seventh century in competition with Kildare and Iona.
Mission 2Diversity

Primacy today

  • Two archbishops of Armagh: the Catholic archbishop and the Church of Ireland (Anglican) archbishop each hold the title Primate of All Ireland; each church's archbishop of Dublin is Primate of Ireland.
  • Both churches see themselves as heirs of Patrick: the claim of continuity matters to both.
  • Presbyterians and other Protestants have no bishops: Patrick's faith and mission, not a see, is his legacy.
  • Two cathedrals named after Patrick stand on two hills in Armagh city.
  • The old contest of claims has become, for many, a symbol of a shared inheritance.
Mission 2Evaluate

Were Armagh's claims valid?

  • Claim: Armagh's claim to primacy rested more on propaganda than on Patrick.
  • For: Patrick never mentions Armagh; the claims appear in the seventh century, in texts written to win churches and dues.
  • For: The claims rose with the Uí Néill; an angel's grant and a royal note are tools of power.
  • Against: A real link to Patrick is plausible; later writers built on an existing tradition, not nothing.
  • Against: Validity in church terms rests also on acceptance: other churches, kings and Rome recognised Armagh; authority can grow legitimately.
  • Against: Promoting a saint's church was normal in the period (Kildare did the same); "propaganda" judges it by modern standards.
  • Judgement criteria: Historical truth of the founding, or legitimacy through acceptance? Can a claim be politically motivated and still valid?
Mission check

?A medieval monastery claims to be the head of a region's churches. Its claim rests on a Life written two centuries after its founder, a charter in which an angel grants the region, and a later king's confirmation. Applying the Armagh debate, which assessment is fairest?

Armagh's primacy grew from a possible link with Patrick, through seventh-century texts, relics, law and royal backing, to recognition by Rome.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Why would a monk leave home forever, sailing off with no plan to return?

Make a guess: Why would a monk leave home forever, sailing off with no plan to return?

Mission 3

Peregrinatio: exile for Christ

  • Peregrinatio (Latin): living as a foreigner, away from home. A peregrinus (plural peregrini) is the person who does it.
  • In early Irish monasticism it meant voluntary, permanent exile "for Christ" (pro Christo) or "for the love of God" (pro amore Dei).
  • Not a round-trip pilgrimage to a shrine: the peregrinus normally did not come back.
  • The sacrifice was real: in Irish society your rights, honour and protection came from your kin and your túath (small kingdom). Leaving them meant becoming nobody.
  • Many Irish peregrini left in the 6th–8th centuries for Scotland, England and the Continent.
Mission 3

Three kinds of martyrdom

  • The Cambrai Homily (an Old Irish sermon, probably late 7th century, in an 8th-century manuscript) names three martyrdoms (paraphrase):
  • White martyrdom (bánmartre): leaving everything you love for God's sake.
  • Glas martyrdom (glasmartre, green or blue): giving up your desires through fasting, labour and penance.
  • Red martyrdom (dergmartre): suffering death for Christ.
  • With persecution over, monks found other ways to give their lives to God. Peregrinatio was the white martyrdom made concrete.
  • Many peregrini lived all three: exile, strict ascetic discipline, and some (Killian) a violent death.
Mission 3Read the source

Strangers on the earth

> "Now the LORD said to Abram, 'Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father's house, and go to the land that I will show you.'" (Genesis 12:1, WEBBE)

> "These all died in faith … and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." (Hebrews 11:13, WEBBE)

  • Irish writers, including Columbanus, used Abraham's call as the pattern of peregrinatio.
  • Jesus' promise to those who leave home "for my name's sake" (Matthew 19:29) gave the same message.

Q1 Which words of Genesis 12:1 match the white martyrdom?

Show answer

Leaving country, relatives and father's house.

Q2 What does Hebrews 11:13 add?

Show answer

The idea that every Christian is a stranger on earth: exile makes visible what is true of all believers.

Mission 3

Background and motives

  • Ascetic: exile as the hardest form of self-denial; imitating Abraham and Christ, who had "nowhere to lay his head" (Matthew 8:20).
  • Penitential: Irish law and the penitentials could impose exile as a penalty; some chose it as penance.
  • Missionary: preaching to pagans or to Christians in need of renewal, in line with Matthew 28:19.
  • Social: Thomas Charles-Edwards (b. 1943), "The social background to Irish peregrinatio" (Celtica, 1976), shows that a peregrinus had no legal standing outside his own túath. Exile overseas was the highest grade.
  • Changing over time: Kathleen Hughes (1926–1977), "The changing theory and practice of Irish pilgrimage" (Journal of Ecclesiastical History, 1960), argues the early ideal was mainly ascetic; mission and later pilgrimage to Rome grew from it.
Quick check
?Which description fits the Irish idea of peregrinatio most precisely?
Mission 3

Colmcille (Columba), c. 521–597

  • Born in Donegal into the Uí Néill, the most powerful royal dynasty in the north.
  • Founded monasteries in Ireland (traditions link him with Derry and Durrow).
  • 563: sailed with twelve companions to Iona, in the Irish kingdom of Dál Riata (western Scotland).
  • His biographer Adomnán (abbot of Iona, Life of Columba, c. 700) says he went pro Christo perigrinari volens, "wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ".
  • A later story (the copied psalter and the battle of Cúl Dreimne, 561) makes exile a penance; Adomnán mentions the battle but does not give it as the reason.
  • Contribution: Iona headed a family (familia, paruchia) of monasteries in Ireland and Scotland; mission to the Picts (Bede says he converted the northern Picts; Adomnán describes his visit to King Bridei); a centre of learning and copying.
Mission 3

Aidan of Lindisfarne, d. 651

  • Oswald became king of Northumbria in 634. He had been in exile among the Irish and baptised in Iona's tradition.
  • He asked Iona for a bishop. Bede (Ecclesiastical History of the English People, 731, III.3, III.5) says the first one sent was harsh, failed and went home.
  • Aidan, a monk of Iona, said the English should first be given the gentle "milk" of teaching (1 Corinthians 3:2). He was sent instead (635).
  • Founded Lindisfarne, a tidal island near the royal fortress of Bamburgh. At first Oswald himself translated his preaching.
  • Walked rather than rode; gave away a fine horse from King Oswine to a beggar (III.14); trained English boys as clergy.
  • Bede, who backed Roman Easter, still praised his life highly (III.17): strong evidence of his reputation.
Mission 3

Colman and the Synod of Whitby

  • Colman: third Irish bishop of Lindisfarne (661–664), after Aidan and Finan.
  • At the Synod of Whitby (664) he defended Iona's way of dating Easter, appealing to the apostle John and to Columba (see Mission 1).
  • King Oswiu chose the Roman practice, because Peter holds the keys.
  • Colman left with the Irish monks and about thirty English monks: first to Iona, then to Inishbofin (Co. Mayo, c. 668).
  • When the Irish and English monks quarrelled (the Irish left for the summer and came back to share the harvest), he founded a separate house at Mayo for the English (Bede IV.4). "Mayo of the Saxons" lasted for centuries.
  • Significance: loyalty to his tradition over power; Irish influence in Northumbria now passed through English disciples.
Quick check
?Bede supported the Roman date of Easter, yet he praised Aidan's way of life very highly. What does this suggest to a historian?
Mission 3

Gall and Killian

  • Gall (c. 550–c. 646): monk of Bangor, companion of Columbanus (see Mission 4) on the Continent.
  • 612: stayed behind near Lake Constance when Columbanus went to Italy; the later Lives of Gall say he was ill and that Columbanus was angry with him.
  • Lived as a hermit on the river Steinach. The Abbey of St Gall (founded on the site in 719) became one of Europe's great centres of learning, with a famous library and Irish manuscripts.
  • Killian (Kilian, d. c. 689): Irish bishop who went with companions Colman (a priest) and Totnan (a deacon) to Würzburg in Franconia.
  • Converted Duke Gozbert. His Passio says he told the duke his marriage to his brother's widow was unlawful; the three were killed (c. 689) on the order of the duchess, Geilana.
  • Red martyrdom: still honoured as patron of Würzburg.
Mission 3

The Burgh Castle Group

  • Fursa (Fursey, d. c. 650), with his brothers Foillan and Ultan and the priests Gobban and Dicuil, came from Ireland to East Anglia (c. 630s).
  • King Sigeberht gave them a site inside an old fort, Cnobheresburg (Bede III.19), usually identified with the Roman shore fort at Burgh Castle (near Great Yarmouth). The identification is traditional, not certain.
  • Fursa was famous for visions of the next life, written down soon after his death and widely copied.
  • He moved on to Gaul (Lagny), died there and was buried at Péronne, later called "Péronne of the Irish". Foillan and Ultan worked in what is now Belgium.
  • Significance: Irish monks supported the conversion of East Anglia alongside the Burgundian bishop Felix; a chain of peregrini linked Ireland, England and Gaul.
Mission 3Diversity

Six peregrini, different paths

  • Ascetic exile first: Colmcille (Adomnán's "pilgrim for Christ"); Gall's hermit life.
  • Invited mission: Aidan, called by a king, working through the king's court.
  • Tradition under pressure: Colman, who chose exile again rather than conform.
  • Frontier mission and martyrdom: Killian among the Franks and Thuringians.
  • Mission, vision and onward exile: Fursa's group, moving from Ireland to England to Gaul.
  • Common thread: monastic bases, not dioceses; abbots and bishops sharing roles; book culture; loyalty to Irish custom.
Mission 3Evaluate

How great was their contribution?

  • Claim: The peregrini were decisive for Christianity in Northern Britain and Europe.
  • For: Iona and Lindisfarne evangelised the Picts and most of Northumbria; Northumbria later sent missionaries to Mercia, Essex and Frisia.
  • For: monasteries such as St Gall, Würzburg and Péronne lasted for centuries as centres of learning and worship.
  • Against: most of Gaul and the Rhineland were already Christian; the peregrini often renewed a church rather than founding one.
  • Against: Roman and Frankish missions mattered too (Augustine in Kent, 597; Felix in East Anglia; Paulinus in Northumbria); Whitby shows the Roman pattern won out.
  • Against: much of our evidence is hagiography written long after (Adomnán, the Lives of Gall, the Passio Kiliani), and Bede had his own agenda ( on reading saints' Lives).
  • Judgement criteria: lasting institutions or first conversions? Contemporary sources or later legend? Whole regions or local impact?
Mission 3Evaluate

Ascetics or missionaries?

  • Claim: The peregrini set out mainly to save their own souls, not to convert others.
  • For: the sources stress exile "for Christ"; the Cambrai Homily frames it as martyrdom; Gall chose the hermit life; Hughes sees mission as a later development.
  • Against: Aidan was invited to preach; Killian sought out pagans; Colmcille's mission to the Picts was active.
  • Middle view: exile and mission were one vocation. A community living in exile drew people to Christ by its way of life; preaching followed.
  • Judgement criteria: stated motives or actual activity? Early or later peregrini? The writer's purpose (a saint's Life praising holiness, or Bede praising mission)?
Mission check

?Around 825, the Irish scholar Dicuil (not the Dicuil of Fursa's group) reported that Irish hermits had lived on remote North Atlantic islands where almost nobody else lived, seeking solitude for God. What does this evidence add to the debate in the earlier screen?

Exile for Christ came first; mission often grew out of it. A later mission: Columbanus, the peregrinus who took on kings and popes.

Mission 4

Mission 4: How did one Irish monk end up defying a queen and lecturing a pope?

Make a guess: How did one Irish monk end up defying a queen and lecturing a pope?

Mission 4

From Leinster to Bangor

  • Columbanus (Columbán, c. 543–615), born in Leinster.
  • Studied scripture under Sinell on Cleenish island (Lough Erne), then became a monk at Bangor (Co. Down) under its founder Comgall.
  • Bangor was known for strict discipline, learning and continuous sung prayer.
  • c. 590/591: in middle age, with twelve companions (among them Gall), he left for Gaul: the white martyrdom of peregrinatio.
  • Main source: Jonas of Bobbio, Life of Columbanus (c. 640), written by a monk who joined Bobbio three years after Columbanus died and used his disciples' memories.
Mission 4

Annegray, Luxeuil, Fontaine

  • A Frankish king of Burgundy gave land in the Vosges hills. Jonas names Sigebert, who was already dead; most historians think of Childebert II or Guntram.
  • Three foundations: Annegray, then Luxeuil (in the ruins of a Roman spa town), then Fontaine.
  • Hundreds came, many from Frankish noble families: the first great monastic movement in that region in a generation.
  • Luxeuil became the mother house. Its abbots and monks later founded or reformed dozens of monasteries (Faremoutiers, Jouarre, Rebais, Corbie, Saint-Bertin).
  • Friedrich Prinz (1928–2003), Frühes Mönchtum im Frankenreich (1965), calls this Hiberno-Frankish monasticism: Irish discipline joined to Frankish aristocratic patronage.
Mission 4

The Rule for Monks

  • Regula Monachorum: ten short chapters, more spiritual teaching than legal code.
  • Topics: obedience, silence, food and drink, poverty, overcoming vanity, chastity, the daily office (prayer in choir), discretion, mortification (dying to self-will), perfection.
  • Obedience comes first: at a senior's word, the monk rises at once to obey (paraphrase, ch. 1).
  • Food is plain and taken in the evening; the monk should go to bed tired and rise before he has slept enough (paraphrase).
  • Discretion (ch. 8): telling good from bad and judging the right measure, so that strictness serves love.
  • Goal: the monk dies to his own will so that Christ may live in him (Galatians 2:20).
Mission 4

The Community Rule and the Penitential

  • Regula Coenobialis (Community Rule): a list of penalties for faults in daily life: forgetting to say "Amen" at grace, talking at meals, spilling food, arriving late to prayer.
  • Penalties include extra psalms, periods of silence, fasting and a set number of blows with a strap.
  • Parts may have been added by his successors at Luxeuil.
  • Penitential of Columbanus: a tariff of penances for monks, clergy and lay people.
  • It brought the Irish practice of private, repeatable confession to the Continent, where public penance (once in a lifetime) had been the norm.
  • Significance: private confession became the common Catholic practice in Western Europe.
Quick check
?Which statement about Columbanus' contribution to monasticism is best supported by the sources?
Mission 4

Religious controversy: Easter and the bishops

  • Columbanus kept the Irish Easter reckoning (an 84-year cycle) and would not adopt the Gaulish one (the cycle of Victorius of Aquitaine).
  • Letter 1 (c. 600) to Pope Gregory the Great: asks him to reject Victorius' cycle, with sharp wit and great respect.
  • He also ran his monasteries without submitting to the local bishops, as Irish abbots did.
  • Letter 2 (603) to the Gaulish bishops gathered in synod (probably at Chalon): he declines to attend. He asks them (paraphrase) to let him live in silence in the woods, beside the graves of his seventeen dead brothers, and to let Gaul hold both traditions, as heaven will.
  • Behind the dispute: who has authority over a monastery founded by foreigners in your diocese?
Mission 4Read the source

Jonas on the confrontation with the king

Jonas, Life of Columbanus I.19 (paraphrase):

  • Queen Brunhild, grandmother of King Theuderic II, brings the king's sons by his concubines to Columbanus for a blessing.
  • He refuses: they are born of unlawful unions, and will never hold the royal sceptre.
  • He also refuses to let the king's men enter the monastery's inner enclosure.
  • Theuderic orders him out of the kingdom (610).

Q1 What two kinds of authority clash here?

Show answer

Royal power over church and family affairs; the abbot's duty to moral law and his monastery's freedom.

Q2 Why might Jonas tell the story this way, writing about 30 years later?

Show answer

To present Columbanus as a prophet confronting a wicked ruler, like John the Baptist before Herod, Mark 6:18; Brunhild's line had fallen, so she was a safe villain.

Mission 4

Exile and Bobbio

  • 610: taken under guard to Nantes to be shipped to Ireland. Jonas says a storm drove the ship back, and he was freed.
  • Welcomed by Chlothar II (Neustria), then by Theudebert II (Austrasia); travelled up the Rhine to Bregenz on Lake Constance (c. 610–612).
  • When Theudebert was defeated (612), he crossed the Alps to Lombard Italy, leaving Gall behind.
  • King Agilulf and Queen Theodelinda gave him land at Bobbio (c. 613), where he died on 23 November 615.
  • Letter 4 (610): to his monks at Luxeuil, written as he was being deported: tender, grieving, urging unity and obedience to Attala.
  • Bobbio received a papal privilege (628) freeing it from the local bishop's control: an early example of monastic exemption.
Mission 4

Letter 5: advising a pope

  • 613: at Agilulf's request he wrote to Pope Boniface IV about the Three Chapters controversy, which had split the churches of northern Italy from Rome.
  • He calls the Irish disciples of Saints Peter and Paul, bound to the chair of Peter (paraphrase), and praises Rome as the head of the churches.
  • He then urges the pope, with startling frankness, to call a synod and clear himself of the suspicion of heresy.
  • He apologises for writing so boldly but claims the freedom of speech of his homeland (paraphrase).
  • Read two ways: loyalty to Rome's primacy, or a claim that even a pope can be called to account by the faith he holds.
Mission 4

His writings

  • Edited by G. S. M. Walker, Sancti Columbani Opera (1957): Latin texts with translation.
  • Letters: six usually accepted (1–2 on Easter and the bishops, 3 to a pope on Easter, 4 to Luxeuil, 5 to Boniface IV, 6 to a young disciple).
  • Instructions (Instructiones, thirteen sermons): human life as a road walked by pilgrims heading home to God (paraphrase).
  • Rules and Penitential.
  • Poems (e.g. to Hunald, Sethus and Fidolius): authorship disputed. Some scholars, including Michael Lapidge, assign some to a later writer of the same name.
  • Significance: the first large body of writing by an Irish author on the Continent: evidence of Irish Latin learning, classical reading and a vivid personality.
Quick check
?Columbanus writes to the pope praising Rome, but urges him to clear himself of suspicion of heresy. Which reading fits this letter best?
Mission 4Evaluate

His contribution to monasticism

  • Claim: Columbanus transformed monasticism in Western Europe.
  • For: Luxeuil and Bobbio spread a monastic movement among the Frankish nobility; dozens of houses traced their origin to him (Prinz).
  • For: private, repeatable confession spread through his Penitential.
  • For: monastic exemption from bishops (Bobbio, 628) became a model.
  • Against: his Rule was too severe to last alone: by the mid-7th century Luxeuil houses used a mixed rule (with Benedict's), and Benedict's Rule replaced it in the 9th century.
  • Against: Jonas wrote to glorify his founder and his successors; the scale of his influence may be inflated (Ian Wood and others on Jonas' purposes).
  • Judgement criteria: lasting institutions or lasting rules? Influence through disciples or through his own texts? How far can a hagiography be trusted?
Mission 4Evaluate

Controversy: prophet or trouble-maker?

  • Claim: Columbanus' conflicts were caused by his own inflexibility.
  • For: he refused to compromise on a calendar issue; he would not attend the bishops' synod; he exasperated Gaulish bishops and a powerful queen.
  • Against: on the king's sons and the enclosure he stood for moral principle and the church's freedom against royal power, like prophets before kings.
  • Against: he asked for peace and coexistence (Letter 2) and showed deep respect for Rome (Letters 1, 5).
  • Context: Merovingian politics were brutal; Brunhild was one of the most powerful rulers of the age. His conflicts also involved royal patronage of monasteries.
  • Judgement criteria: consistency with his own principles? Willingness to compromise? Reliability of Jonas, who had reasons to blacken Brunhild?
Mission 4Evaluate

The writings: impact and significance

  • Claim: Columbanus' writings matter more for what they show of him than for their influence.
  • For: the letters reveal a person (humour, anger, grief, humility, boldness) as few early medieval sources do.
  • For: the Instructions and poems were read far less widely than Gregory or Benedict.
  • Against: the Rules and Penitential shaped monastic and penitential practice for centuries.
  • Against: Letters 1 and 5 show the Irish church's loyalty to Rome and its independence in custom: key evidence for church history.
  • Later significance: often called a "father of Europe". Letter 1 includes an early use of "Europe" for the Christian West, and Robert Schuman praised him at Luxeuil in 1950 as an inspiration for European unity.
  • Judgement criteria: influence in his own time or later? Disputed works in or out? Practice or ideas?
Mission check

?About 630, a Frankish bishop complains that the monks of a Columbanian house will not let him enter their enclosure or impose his customs, though they honour the pope. Which principle of Columbanus does their stance best reflect?

Columbanus' fierce independence was never a rejection of authority: it was an appeal to a higher one. Next: controversy and reform in the Reformation era.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Who has the final say in the church: the Bible, the Pope, the bishops or the people?

Make a guess: Who has the final say in the church: the Bible, the Pope, the bishops or the people?

Mission 5

Authority in the late medieval church

  • One Western church, headed by the Pope as successor of Peter (Matthew 16:18), with bishops, canon law and seven sacraments ministered by priests.
  • Authority lay in Scripture and the church's tradition, interpreted by the Pope, bishops and councils.
  • Strains by 1500:
  • The Western Schism (1378–1417): two, then three, rival popes. The Council of Constance (1414–1418) ended it, and conciliarists argued a general council stood above a pope.
  • Abuses widely criticised: absent bishops, poorly trained clergy, buying of church offices, the sale of indulgences.
  • Reformers before Luther: John Wyclif (d. 1384), Jan Hus (burned 1415).
Mission 5

Luther's challenge

  • Martin Luther (1483–1546), Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg.
  • 1517: Ninety-Five Theses against the preaching of indulgences.
  • 1519 (Leipzig Debate): denies that popes and councils cannot err.
  • Sola scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority over church tradition; sola fide, sola gratia: salvation by faith and grace, not merit.
  • 1520: To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation: all baptised Christians belong to the "spiritual estate"; the difference between clergy and laity is one of office only (paraphrase).
  • 1521: excommunicated; refused to recant at the Diet of Worms unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason.
Mission 5Read the source

A royal priesthood

> "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light." (1 Peter 2:9, WEBBE)

  • Luther read this as the basis of the priesthood of all believers: every Christian has direct access to God and a calling to serve.
  • Catholic teaching also uses 1 Peter 2:9 (the common priesthood of the faithful), but holds that the ordained priesthood differs in kind, not only in office (restated at Vatican II).

Q1 To whom is the letter addressed: clergy or the whole church?

Show answer

The whole church: "you" are the chosen race.

Q2 Why does the verse matter for church organisation?

Show answer

If all are priests, authority can pass to congregations, elders or rulers, not only to ordained clergy.

Mission 5

New church orders on the Continent

  • Lutheran: territorial churches under the prince; superintendents often replaced bishops (Sweden kept bishops in succession). The Augsburg Confession (1530) defined belief.
  • Peace of Augsburg (1555): each ruler chose the region's faith, later summed up as cuius regio, eius religio ("whose realm, his religion").
  • Reformed: John Calvin (1509–1564), Ecclesiastical Ordinances for Geneva (1541): four offices: pastors, doctors (teachers), elders, deacons. A Consistory of pastors and elders oversaw discipline.
  • This became the presbyterian model: government by ministers and elders in courts (session, presbytery, synod, assembly). John Knox brought it to Scotland (1560).
  • In Ireland: the first presbytery met at Carrickfergus (1642); today's Presbyterian Church in Ireland follows this pattern.
Mission 5

England, Ireland and the Radical Reformation

  • England: Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534) made the king Supreme Head of the Church; Elizabeth I (1559) took the title Supreme Governor.
  • Bishops, dioceses and parishes kept; the Book of Common Prayer and the Thirty-Nine Articles (1571) set worship and doctrine.
  • Ireland: the Irish Parliament passed its own Act of Supremacy (1537). The established Church of Ireland kept episcopal order, but most people stayed Catholic.
  • Radical Reformation: Anabaptists (e.g. the Schleitheim Confession, 1527): believers' baptism, gathered congregations choosing their own pastors, separation from the state. Ancestors of Mennonites and, indirectly, of later Baptist churches.
  • Result: authority now lay variously in Scripture, rulers, ministers and elders, or the congregation.
Quick check
?Which pairing of a Reformation church with its way of government is correct?
Mission 5

The Council of Trent, 1545–1563

  • Called by Pope Paul III; met in three periods over 18 years.
  • Authority (Session IV, 1546): the council received Scripture and the unwritten traditions "with an equal affection of piety, and reverence" (Waterworth's 1848 translation). The Church judges the true sense of Scripture; the Vulgate declared authentic.
  • Doctrine: justification (Session VI, 1547) and the seven sacraments reaffirmed against Protestant views.
  • Organisation: bishops must reside in their dioceses and preach; a seminary in every diocese (Session XXIII, 1563); abuses of indulgences condemned (their sale was banned in 1567).
  • Afterwards: the Roman Catechism (1566) and Roman Missal (1570) brought one teaching and one form of Mass across the Latin church.
Mission 5

Rome at the centre

  • Jesuits (Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola, approved 1540): education, missions abroad, special obedience to the Pope.
  • Roman Inquisition (1542) and Index of forbidden books (1559) policed doctrine.
  • Sixtus V (1588) organised the Roman Curia into permanent congregations: more decisions taken in Rome.
  • Trent's decrees were carried out by model bishops such as Charles Borromeo in Milan.
  • Ireland: under the penal laws, Tridentine reforms came slowly. Irish colleges abroad (Louvain, Rome, Paris, Salamanca) trained priests; the Synod of Thurles (1850) under Archbishop Paul Cullen applied Trent's discipline across Ireland.
  • Overall: a more centralised, uniform, clergy-led church.
Quick check
?Which statement about the Council of Trent's view of authority is correct?
Mission 5Diversity

Counter-Reformation or Catholic Reformation?

  • Counter-Reformation: Catholic renewal as a reaction against Protestantism (Inquisition, Index, polemic).
  • Catholic Reformation: renewal already under way before Luther (e.g. Cardinal Ximenes in Spain, new orders, humanist scholars), growing from within.
  • Hubert Jedin (1900–1980), Katholische Reformation oder Gegenreformation? (1946): both were real; Trent combined self-reform and defence.
  • John W. O'Malley (1927–2022), Trent and All That (2000), proposes Early Modern Catholicism: a broader label covering missions, art, education and spirituality as well as reaction.
  • Protestant and Catholic historians still weigh these differently. The label you choose shapes how you judge Trent's impact.
Mission 5

From Vatican I to Vatican II

  • Vatican I (1869–1870), Pastor Aeternus: the Pope's universal jurisdiction and infallibility when he defines faith or morals ex cathedra. The council ended early (war in 1870) before it could treat the bishops.
  • Vatican II (1962–1965): announced by Pope John XXIII (1959), completed under Paul VI.
  • Two watchwords: aggiornamento (bringing up to date) and ressourcement (return to the sources: Scripture, the Fathers, the liturgy).
  • Sixteen documents, including four constitutions: on the Church (Lumen Gentium), revelation (Dei Verbum), the liturgy (Sacrosanctum Concilium), and the Church in the modern world (Gaudium et Spes).
Mission 5

Vatican II: organisation and authority

  • Lumen Gentium: the Church first as the People of God (ch. 2), then its hierarchy (ch. 3); collegiality: bishops together, with and under the Pope, share responsibility for the whole Church; a universal call to holiness; the laity's own mission.
  • Dei Verbum: Scripture and tradition flow from one source; the teaching office "is not above the word of God, but serves it" (DV 10).
  • Sacrosanctum Concilium: the vernacular allowed in the Mass; full, active participation of the people.
  • Structures: the Synod of Bishops (1965), national bishops' conferences, parish and pastoral councils, the permanent diaconate restored, lay ministries.
  • Relations: ecumenism (Unitatis Redintegratio), religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae), other religions (Nostra Aetate).
  • Papal primacy and Vatican I's teaching were reaffirmed, not removed.
Mission 5Evaluate

Which change mattered most?

  • Claim: The Reformation changed church organisation and authority more than Trent or Vatican II.
  • For: it broke one Western church into many, each with a different seat of authority (Scripture with prince, presbytery, congregation or monarch).
  • For: the priesthood of all believers and vernacular Bibles shifted authority towards ordinary believers.
  • Against: Trent shaped Catholic structure (seminaries, resident bishops, Roman centralisation) for four centuries, in the largest Christian church.
  • Against: Vatican II changed the daily life of over a billion Catholics (worship in their own language, lay roles, ecumenism) and shaped other churches' dialogue with Rome.
  • Judgement criteria: depth of change or breadth? Structures or attitudes? Short-term impact or lasting? Whose perspective (Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox, secular historian)?
Mission 5Evaluate

Vatican II: reform or rupture?

  • Claim: Vatican II changed the Catholic understanding of authority, not only its style.
  • For: collegiality, the People of God and religious freedom moved away from a top-down, Rome-only model; some traditionalists (e.g. Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, whose 1988 consecrations were declared schismatic) saw a break.
  • Against: the council reaffirmed papal primacy; Paul VI's Humanae Vitae (1968) showed authority still rested with the Pope.
  • Against: Pope Benedict XVI (2005) spoke of a "hermeneutic of reform" in continuity, against a "hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture".
  • Ongoing: Pope Francis' emphasis on synodality (Synod on Synodality, 2021–2024) is seen by some as fulfilling the council, by others as a new step.
  • Judgement criteria: texts or practice? Continuity of doctrine or change of emphasis? Whose reception: bishops, laity, other churches?
Mission check

?In 2023, lay women and men took part as full voting members alongside bishops at an assembly of the Synod of Bishops in Rome, though the Pope kept the final decision. Which earlier development does this most directly build on?

Each reform answered "who has the final say?" differently: Scripture with rulers or elders; Scripture and tradition under Rome; the whole People of God with the Pope. Next: how religion relates to the state.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Easter's date depends on moon, equinox and Sunday; churches used different tables (84-year, 19-year, Victorius, Dionysius).
  • Southern Irish conformed c. 630 (Cummian); the north and Iona later (716); in Northumbria, Whitby (664) ruled for Rome after Wilfrid's appeal to Peter; Colmán left.
  • Whitby's significance is debated: a Roman victory (Bede's story) or a quarrel over custom between churches in communion.

Mission 2

  • Patrick never mentions Armagh; a link is plausible near Emain Macha but unproved.
  • Muirchú, Tírechán and the Liber Angeli (seventh century) claimed all Ireland for Patrick's church, against Kildare, Iona and Clonmacnoise; the Book of Armagh (c. 807) gathered them.
  • Promotion through relics, the Law of Patrick, Uí Néill and Brian Bóruma (1005); recognised at Kells (1152); validity debated: propaganda or legitimate growth.

Mission 3

  • Peregrinatio was permanent, voluntary exile for Christ: the "white martyrdom", modelled on Abraham (Genesis 12:1).
  • Motives mixed asceticism, penance and mission; Charles-Edwards (legal status) and Hughes (changing ideal) explain the background.
  • Colmcille (Iona, Picts), Aidan (Lindisfarne), Colman (Whitby, Inishbofin, Mayo), Gall (St Gall), Killian (Würzburg) and the Burgh Castle Group (East Anglia, Gaul) shaped Christianity across Northern Britain and Europe.

Mission 4

  • Columbanus (c. 543–615), from Bangor, founded Annegray, Luxeuil, Fontaine and Bobbio; his Rules and Penitential spread strict Irish discipline and private confession.
  • His conflicts with Gaulish bishops (Easter, independence) and with Theuderic II and Brunhild (morality, the enclosure) led to exile in 610.
  • His letters, sermons and rules show loyalty to Rome joined to bold freedom of speech; evaluate them with care for Jonas' purposes.

Mission 5

  • The Reformation moved authority to Scripture alone, exercised through princes, monarchs, ministers and elders, or congregations.
  • Trent affirmed Scripture and tradition interpreted by the Church, and built a centralised, clergy-led Catholic structure (seminaries, resident bishops, Curia).
  • Vatican II added collegiality, the People of God, lay roles and vernacular worship, while reaffirming papal primacy: reform or rupture is still debated.
